clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic mutations in DCLRE1C encoding Artemis, an endonuclease essential for opening DNA hairpin coding ends during V(D)J recombination and for general non-homologous end-joining DNA repair.
Immunophenotype is T-B-NK+, indistinguishable at the subset level from RAG deficiency, because both T and B cells fail to rearrange antigen receptors while NK cells are preserved.
The defining feature is cellular radiosensitivity: because Artemis also repairs double-strand DNA breaks, patient cells are hypersensitive to ionising radiation and alkylating agents.

Radiosensitivity increases the risk of conditioning-related toxicity, late effects such as growth impairment and dental abnormalities, and secondary malignancy, so reduced-intensity or reduced-toxicity conditioning is preferred.
It is notably prevalent among Navajo and Apache (Athabascan-speaking) populations owing to a founder mutation.
Presents in early infancy like other SCIDs with failure to thrive, opportunistic infection, chronic diarrhoea and candidiasis.
Ionising radiation, including unnecessary diagnostic imaging, should be minimised given the underlying DNA-repair defect.
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative but conditioning must be tailored to the radiosensitive phenotype; gene therapy is under development.
reference.pathophysiology: Artemis is a nuclease that, once phosphorylated by the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit, opens the covalently sealed DNA hairpins formed at coding ends during V(D)J recombination and participates more broadly in the non-homologous end-joining pathway that repairs DNA double-strand breaks. When Artemis is absent, the double-strand breaks introduced by the RAG recombinase at the immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor loci cannot be resolved, so antigen-receptor assembly fails and both T-cell and B-cell development are arrested, giving the T-B-NK+ pattern with natural killer cells spared. Crucially, because non-homologous end-joining is a ubiquitous DNA-repair mechanism, the defect extends beyond lymphocytes: all cells are impaired in repairing double-strand breaks, conferring hypersensitivity to ionising radiation and radiomimetic chemotherapy. This radiosensitivity underlies the heightened toxicity of standard myeloablative conditioning and the increased long-term risk of growth, dental and malignancy complications, distinguishing Artemis deficiency from the phenotypically similar but radioresistant RAG deficiencies.
additionalDifferentials: RAG1 and RAG2 deficiency (same T-B-NK+ immunophenotype but radioresistant)
DNA ligase IV deficiency (radiosensitive, with microcephaly and dysmorphism)
DNA-PKcs (PRKDC) deficiency, another radiosensitive T-B-NK+ SCID
Ataxia-telangiectasia and other broader DNA-repair syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Lymphocyte subset flow cytometry confirming the T-B-NK+ pattern
Radiosensitivity assay measuring impaired double-strand break repair in patient fibroblasts or lymphocytes
Serum immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses (accounting for maternal IgG)
T-cell receptor repertoire analysis showing absent or restricted diversity
DCLRE1C gene sequencing to confirm the mutation and consider founder variants
Assessment for maternal T-cell engraftment as a confounder
HLA typing of patient and family for transplant planning with radiosensitivity-adapted conditioning
redFlags: Opportunistic or overwhelming infection with failure to thrive in early infancy
Absent thymic shadow with impalpable lymphoid tissue
Excessive toxicity following radiation exposure or alkylating chemotherapy
Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease after non-irradiated cellular blood products
T-B-NK+ SCID immunophenotype in an infant of Athabascan (Navajo or Apache) ancestry
reference.prognosis: Untreated the disorder is fatal in infancy, and even after successful transplantation the underlying DNA-repair defect predisposes to long-term complications including growth and dental abnormalities and secondary malignancy. Reduced-toxicity conditioning improves survival while limiting radiosensitivity-related late effects.
pitfalls: Subset analysis cannot distinguish Artemis from RAG deficiency; a radiosensitivity assay or genetic testing is required.
Standard myeloablative conditioning can cause severe toxicity if the radiosensitive diagnosis is missed before transplant.
Unnecessary diagnostic ionising radiation may cause harm given the systemic DNA-repair defect.
Maternal IgG can mask the humoral defect and maternal engraftment can obscure T-cell absence.
Live vaccines and non-irradiated cellular blood products are hazardous once SCID is suspected.
references: International primary immunodeficiency classification and management guidelines
National newborn screening and SCID management guidance
management: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the curative treatment and should be undertaken promptly in infancy
Use reduced-toxicity conditioning and avoid alkylating agents and irradiation because of the underlying cellular radiosensitivity
Protective isolation, avoidance of live vaccines, and irradiated CMV-safe leucodepleted blood products
Antimicrobial prophylaxis against Pneumocystis, fungi and viruses with agents such as co-trimoxazole, an antifungal and an antiviral
Immunoglobulin replacement therapy to bridge humoral deficiency pending immune reconstitution
Nutritional support for failure to thrive and treatment of chronic diarrhoea and mucocutaneous candidiasis
Long-term surveillance for radiosensitivity-related late effects, including growth and dental abnormalities and secondary malignancy, minimising further diagnostic radiation
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive DCLRE1C disorder, with carrier testing for the Athabascan founder variant and newborn screening for at-risk families
